newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Warring sides agree ceasefire in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Warring sides agree ceasefire in Tajikistan.

text.p: Tajik President Imamali Rakhmonov and Islamic opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri agreed during talks in Afghanistan to a ceasefire between their forces from midnight on Wednesday, a senior Tajik official said.
"Both sides have agreed to cease hostilities from midnight (1900 GMT) tonight," Zafar Saidov, spokesman for Rakhmonov, told Reuters by telephone in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Saidov said the deal would last at least until December 19 when Rakhmonov and Nuri are expected to meet in Moscow to sign a peace accord.
No details have been given on the proposed accord but an aide to Nuri, cited by Russia's Interfax news agency on Tuesday, said some form of a coalition government was considered.
Saidov said opposition fighters had agreed to withdraw from the towns of Komsomolabad, Tajikabad and Jirgadal in the east of the country.
He said both sides had called on United Nations military observers based in Tajikistan to help observe the ceasefire.
"The president believes the ceasefire is a big achievement," Saidov said.
Previous ceasefire agreements sponsored by the United Nations have been routinely flouted.
Fighting flared in the former Soviet republic after the talks were announced last month as each side moved to beef up its bargaining position at the negotiating table.
In a separate development the Tajik interior ministry said a Russian servicemen based in Dushanbe was shot dead on his way home late on Tuesday.

The killing follows a spate of attacks, widely blamed on the opposition, against Russian troops, thousands of whom fulfil peacekeeping duties, guard the country's southern border with Afghanistan and help shore up Rakhmonov's shaky government.
The opposition has never formally claimed attacks on Russian servicemen in Tajikistan.

The four-year civil war has left tens of thousands dead and made many more homeless in the remote, mountainous country where regional and clan rivalries underlie the conflict between the secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
